Stipulation

/stip-yuh-LAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Stipulation means a specific condition or requirement that is formally demanded as part of an agreement.

Stipulation means a specific condition or requirement that is formally demanded as part of an agreement. The scholarship came with one stipulation: recipients had to maintain at least a B average every semester.

Worked Example

A touring band signed a contract to headline a summer festival. Buried in the paperwork was a stipulation that the band perform at least ninety minutes, rain or shine. When a storm rolled in and the band cut its set to an hour, the festival withheld part of the payment. The whole dispute came down to that single written condition both sides had agreed to.

The contract contained one formally required condition (the ninety-minute set), which is exactly what a stipulation is.

How Stipulation Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

condition

condition: a requirement that must be met before something else happens

proviso

proviso: a clause in an agreement that introduces a condition

Antonyms

waiver

waiver: an official decision to give up or excuse a requirement

How Strong Is It? — suggestion → stipulation → ultimatum

suggestion vs. stipulation

suggestion vs. stipulation: A suggestion merely proposes what someone might do, while a stipulation is a condition formally required by an agreement.

ultimatum vs. stipulation

ultimatum vs. stipulation: A stipulation sets a required term within a deal, but an ultimatum is a final demand backed by the threat of ending the deal altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stipul

Root — stipul: from Latin stipulari, to demand a formal promise

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Stipulation comes from Latin stipulari, 'to demand a formal promise,' a term from Roman contract law. One old legend ties it to stipula, 'a straw,' from a supposed custom of breaking a straw to seal a bargain, though scholars consider that origin uncertain.

Use the root in a new word: stipulate

Use the root in a new word: stipulate: The lease stipulates that tenants give sixty days' notice, using the verb form of the same Latin root for demanding a formal promise.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal, legal/contractual register

Stipulation usually appears in the patterns 'with the stipulation that' or 'a stipulation in the contract.' It names one specific required term inside an agreement, not the whole agreement itself.
